title: Model & App Deployment
blurb: Run applications and models reliably in production: service boundaries, configuration, health, artifacts, observability, scaling, and runtime safety.

intermediate: Serving an ML model as an API

lessons.title: From local code to a production service
lessons.explain: Deployment turns local code into a reliable service other people or systems can call. Define a stable service interface, package the runtime, externalize configuration, expose health signals, and verify startup/shutdown behavior.
objectives: Turn local code into a callable service
Identify runtime requirements separate from CI/CD automation
Explain how service interface changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect service interface with runtime packaging and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Deploying code that works locally without accounting for environment differences (dependencies, config) between local and production.
lessons.explanation: Deployment turns local code into a reliable service other people or systems can call. Define a stable service interface, package the runtime, externalize configuration, expose health signals, and verify startup/shutdown behavior.

lessons.title: Service contracts, health checks & readiness
objectives: Separate liveness from readiness
Design health endpoints that do not lie about dependencies
Explain how liveness changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect liveness with readiness and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A deployed service needs a clear contract and health signals. Liveness answers whether the process is alive; readiness answers whether it can safely receive traffic.
commonMistakes: Returning “healthy” before required startup work is complete can send real traffic to a service that cannot serve it.
lessons.explain: A deployed service needs a clear contract and health signals. Liveness answers whether the process is alive; readiness answers whether it can safely receive traffic.

lessons.title: Deployment Prerequisites: Containers & Configuration
objectives: Explain what a container provides
Explain how container changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect container with portable and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before continuing in Deployment, you should already be comfortable with what's covered in the Docker course: a container packages an application together with its dependencies and runtime, making it portable across machines -- this is exactly why "it works on my machine" becomes less of a problem.
examples:

# - configure environment variables and container networking
#
# If any of this is unfamiliar, review the Docker course first --
# Deployment picks up from here: shipping that container safely.
commonMistakes: Skipping straight into CI/CD and release strategy without solid Docker fundamentals -- Deployment assumes containerization is already comfortable, and gaps there make the actual Deployment.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing what you're expected to already know is as useful as the content itself -- this checkpoint exists so the rest of Deployment can focus entirely on what it actually owns.

lessons.title: Environment variables & configuration
objectives: Use environment variables to separate configuration from code
Explain how environment variables changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect environment variables with configuration and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Environment variables store configuration (API keys, database URLs, feature flags) OUTSIDE the codebase itself, so the same code can run differently in development, staging, and production just by changing the environment it runs in -- without ever hardcoding secrets or environment-specific values directly into source code.
examples:
import os
database_url = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')
api_key = os.environ.get('API_KEY')
# the SAME code runs against different databases/keys per environment
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a secret or environment-specific value (like a production database URL) directly into source code -- this leaks into version control and can't differ across environments.
lessons.careerRelevance: Separating configuration from code via environment variables is a basic, expected practice in any real deployed application.
lessons.explain: Environment variables store configuration (API keys, database URLs, feature flags) OUTSIDE the codebase itself, so the same code can run differently in development, staging, and production just by changing the environment it runs in -- without ever hardcoding secrets or environment-specific values directly into source code.
lessons.example:
import os
database_url = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')
api_key = os.environ.get('API_KEY')
# the SAME code runs against different databases/keys per environment

lessons.title: Artifacts, model loading & startup lifecycle
objectives: Version runtime artifacts
Load large artifacts once at startup
Fail fast when required artifacts are invalid
lessons.explanation: Production services often depend on model weights, indexes, templates, or other versioned artifacts. Load expensive immutable artifacts during startup rather than once per request, validate their version/checksum, and make startup fail clearly if a required artifact is missing or incompatible.
examples:
from pathlib import Path
MODEL = Path('model.bin')
if not MODEL.exists():
    raise RuntimeError('required model artifact missing')
# load once during startup, then reuse for requests
commonMistakes: Loading a large model or index on every request destroys latency and can exhaust memory under concurrency.
lessons.explain: Production services often depend on model weights, indexes, templates, or other versioned artifacts. Load expensive immutable artifacts during startup rather than once per request, validate their version/checksum, and make startup fail clearly if a required artifact is missing or incompatible.

lessons.title: Logging in production
objectives: Explain why structured, leveled logging matters in production
Explain how logging changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect logging with log levels and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Once code is running in production, you can't attach a debugger to it the way you can locally -- logging is often your only window into what actually happened.
examples:
import logging
logging.info('Order %s processed successfully', order_id)
logging.error('Payment failed for order %s: %s', order_id, error_message)
commonMistakes: Relying only on print statements in a deployed production system -- these aren't leveled, searchable, or aggregable the way real logging is.
lessons.careerRelevance: Production-quality logging is what makes a real deployed system's problems actually debuggable after the fact.
lessons.explain: Once code is running in production, you can't attach a debugger to it the way you can locally -- logging is often your only window into what actually happened.
lessons.example:
import logging
logging.info('Order %s processed successfully', order_id)
logging.error('Payment failed for order %s: %s', order_id, error_message)

lessons.title: Monitoring & alerting
objectives: Explain what monitoring and alerting provide in production
Explain how monitoring changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect monitoring with alerting and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Monitoring continuously tracks a system's health (error rates, response times, resource usage) so problems can be noticed proactively, rather than only when a user complains.
examples:
# example alert rule:
# if error_rate > 5% for more than 2 minutes -> page the on-call engineer
# without this, the team might not notice until customers start complaining
commonMistakes: Having no automated alerting and relying on customers or manual dashboard-checking to notice real production problems.
lessons.careerRelevance: Monitoring and alerting are what let a real engineering team respond to production issues quickly, not just eventually.
lessons.explain: Monitoring continuously tracks a system's health (error rates, response times, resource usage) so problems can be noticed proactively, rather than only when a user complains.

lessons.title: Scaling workers, concurrency & resource limits
objectives: Choose a worker/concurrency model
Set explicit resource limits
Recognize CPU-bound vs I/O-bound serving constraints
lessons.explanation: Scaling is not just adding replicas. Decide how many requests one process can safely handle, whether work is CPU-bound or I/O-bound, how much memory each worker consumes, and when horizontal replicas are safer than increasing concurrency inside one process.
examples:
workers = 4
memory_per_worker_mb = 700
print('estimated memory MB:', workers * memory_per_worker_mb)
commonMistakes: Increasing worker count without measuring memory or CPU can make a service slower or cause out-of-memory restarts.
lessons.explain: Scaling is not just adding replicas. Decide how many requests one process can safely handle, whether work is CPU-bound or I/O-bound, how much memory each worker consumes, and when horizontal replicas are safer than increasing concurrency inside one process.

lessons.title: Timeouts, graceful shutdown & runtime failure
objectives: Use timeouts around external calls
Stop accepting new work during shutdown
Let in-flight work finish or cancel safely
lessons.explanation: Production processes are restarted, rescheduled, and terminated. External calls need timeouts so requests cannot hang forever, and shutdown should stop new work before releasing resources.
examples:
# shutdown sequence, conceptually:
# 1. mark readiness = false
# 2. stop accepting new requests
# 3. wait briefly for in-flight work
# 4. close clients/files and exit
commonMistakes: Ignoring termination signals can drop in-flight requests and leave external resources in an uncertain state.
lessons.explain: Production processes are restarted, rescheduled, and terminated. External calls need timeouts so requests cannot hang forever, and shutdown should stop new work before releasing resources.

lessons.title: Post-deploy smoke tests & runtime validation
objectives: Verify a deployed service through its public boundary
Check critical dependencies and one realistic request
Separate deployment validation from the CI pipeline itself
lessons.explanation: After a service starts, validate the actual deployed runtime: call the health/readiness endpoints, send one realistic request through the public interface, verify a critical dependency, and confirm logs/metrics appear. CI/CD decides how a release is delivered; smoke validation proves the running instance actually works.
examples:
# conceptual smoke checks
checks = ['GET /health -> 200', 'GET /ready -> 200', 'POST /predict sample -> valid schema', 'metric emitted']
for check in checks:
    print('verify:', check)
commonMistakes: Treating “the deployment command succeeded” as proof the application is usable misses startup, dependency, and routing failures.
lessons.explain: After a service starts, validate the actual deployed runtime: call the health/readiness endpoints, send one realistic request through the public interface, verify a critical dependency, and confirm logs/metrics appear. CI/CD decides how a release is delivered; smoke validation proves the running instance actually works.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between blue-green deployment and canary release, and when would you choose one over the other?
interviewPreparation.a: Blue-green switches all traffic at once between two full environments, with instant rollback by switching back -- simple, but a bad release still affects 100% of users the moment it's live. Canary ramps gradually (5%, 25%, 100%), catching problems while only a fraction of users are affected, at the cost of more complexity and a slower rollout. Canary is usually preferred when the blast radius of a bad release matters more than rollout speed.

interviewPreparation.q: How do feature flags change the relationship between deploying and releasing?
interviewPreparation.a: They decouple the two: code can be deployed to production dark (present but inactive) and released to users separately, gradually, or instantly reverted by flipping the flag off -- no new deploy needed. This means a bad feature can be turned off in seconds instead of requiring a rollback deploy.

interviewPreparation.q: A canary release looked healthy the whole time but a bad version still reached all users. What would you investigate?
interviewPreparation.a: Whether the health checks and canary duration actually matched the failure mode -- a canary that only runs for a minute won't catch a slow memory leak or a failure that only appears under sustained load. The canary process needs to run long enough, and check the right signals, for the specific ways this deploy could actually fail.

interviewPreparation.q: Why might 'the server responds to a health check' not be a sufficient signal that a release is actually healthy?
interviewPreparation.a: A server can respond to a basic ping while a specific endpoint is broken, a downstream dependency is failing, or error rates are elevated on real traffic -- a shallow health check only proves the process is running, not that it's doing its job correctly. Real health checks should reflect the actual behavior you care about, not just process liveness.

interviewPreparation.q: What makes a rollback plan trustworthy versus just theoretical?
interviewPreparation.a: Having actually exercised it -- triggered a real rollback in a non-production or staging environment and confirmed the previous version came back correctly, rather than assuming it would work because the steps are documented. A rollback procedure that's never been tested is one of the most common things that fails exactly when you need it most.

careerApplications: Turns a working model/app into something a company can actually ship.

capstone.title: Ship a safe, observable release pipeline for your deployed system
capstone.description: Take the system you've already deployed to the cloud (from the Cloud Computing capstone, or equivalent) and build the release layer on top of it: an automated CI pipeline that tests and deploys on merge, a release strategy that limits blast radius (blue-green or canary), health checks that can actually catch a bad release, and a documented rollback you've genuinely exercised. This capstone is deliberately NOT about containerizing, provisioning cloud infrastructure, or writing unit tests -- those are already covered by Docker, Cloud Computing, and Testing. It's specifically about the safety and observability of shipping changes to something already running.
deliverables: A CI pipeline (e.g. GitHub Actions) that runs tests and deploys automatically on merge to main -- not a manual deploy
A release strategy limiting blast radius (blue-green or a canary ramp), not a straight 100% cutover
Health checks specific enough to actually catch a bad release, not just 'the server responds to a ping'
Structured logging and at least one real alert configured on a meaningful signal (error rate, latency), not just 'server is up/down'
A rollback you've actually exercised (not just described) -- a written account of triggering it and confirming the previous version was genuinely restored
capstone.portfolioTips: Actually exercising the rollback -- not just writing that you 'could' roll back -- is the single most convincing piece of evidence here. Anyone can claim a rollback plan exists; showing you actually triggered one and it worked is a different, much stronger signal.

industryUsage.usage: Pioneered much of the industry's thinking on canary releases and automated health-check-driven rollouts, given the cost of a bad release reaching its full user base directly and immediately.
Uses feature flags extensively to decouple deploying code from releasing features to users, letting code ship dark and get turned on gradually or instantly reverted without a new deploy.

Operates release pipelines at a scale where blast-radius control (canary rollouts, staged releases) is a practical necessity, not a nice-to-have, given how many users a single bad release could otherwise reach immediately.
